parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK technician: What are your day-to-day responsibilities and what tasks do you need this new service to handle for managing the drone fleet?

I keep drones and charging equipment in working order by adding new drones, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send them to charge. Repairs and servicing are carried out by me, and regulators can ask us to show how our drones have been looked after. I do not know what tasks we need this new service to handle, as I do not know anything about software.
ASK dispatcher: What are your day-to-day responsibilities and how do you plan, assign, and monitor drone jobs?

I plan and run our flights as a dispatcher, which makes me the licensed person responsible for each flight. My duties include deciding which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves and can call it off. When planning, I might have several dispatchers working at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and while software never chooses a drone or way for us, I do want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. People and devices outside my company report things like whether a load is ready or if the drone reaches its job points and arrives.
ASK desk: What are your day-to-day responsibilities at the airspace desk and how do you interact with the authorities, dispatchers, and airspace information?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace by managing the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When the authorities announce planned closures with a start and end time or sudden closures that apply at once, I enter them into the system. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves, and I want to know how much disruption any closure caused across customers.
